items.title: The rest of the world does names differently.
items.description: Let's explore a world of names. And you can start speaking a new language in 3 weeks with Babbel 🎉. Get 20% OFF a Lifetime subscription ➡️ https://bit.ly/RobWordsSept Our names aren't normal. The structure of [first name] + [optional middle name] + [family name] is not how much of the world does it. Other cultures squeeze in extra information such as tribal names, ancestral villages, nicknames, and even grandparents' names. Many don't include a family name at all. In this video, Rob explores naming conventions from across the globe. Places covered include Japan, Korea, Vietnam, China, Greece, India, Portugal, Spain, Iceland and Russia. By the end of it, you may well be wishing your parents had called you something a little more informative! 👕COOL TSHIRTS: https://robwords.com/shop ⭐️PATREON COMMUNITY: https://patreon.com/robwords 📝FREE NEWSLETTER: https://www.robwords.com/newsletter Check me out on the web, on Twitter & TikTok: https://robwords.com https://x.com/robwordsYT https://tiktok.com/@robwords

items.description: Visit https://hensonshaving.com/robwords or use code "robwords" to get 100 free blades with the purchase of a Henson razor. And watch this video to discover where Henson and hundreds of other surnames came from! Our last names reveal the lives of our ancestors. items.description: Let's explore the mysterious Norn language. Learn a language using the content you love with Migaku. items.title: Why we don't have a sarcasm mark
items.description: Explore lost punctuation‽ Yes please. And see how language shapes perspectives with Ground News. Use my link to get 40% off the Vantage plan: https://ground.news/robwords Why is there no punctuation mark for irony? Or to flag up a rhetorical question? Well, the fact is: there once was. Numerous innovative marks have been invented then discarded ( although you can still find them if you look hard enough). items.title: Are these words really "untranslatable" into English?
items.description: Let's bust some "untranslatable" myths! And remember: learning a language is easier when you practice real conversations. Preply connects you with 1-on-1 tutors. Get 50% off your first lesson with code "ROB50" here: https://preply.sjv.io/m4N6ND The internet loves “untranslatable” words: hygge, saudade, lagom, mamihlapinatapai, and plenty more. But do these words really mean what the listicles say they mean? Are they even real? In this video, let's fact-check some of the world’s most famous supposedly untranslatable words, from Swedish and German to Malay, Dutch, Yaghan, French, Swahili and beyond. Some turn out to be genuine linguistic gems; others are exaggerations, misunderstandings, or outright nonsense. items.title: The hidden logic behind #, @, & and §
items.description: Let's explore where #@&§ came from. And download the Opera browser for free here: https://opr.as/06-Opera-browser-robwords and enjoy its many handy features. Did you know #, &, @, § and ¶ are all made up of letters? In fact, they each represent specific words. In this video, I'll explain where these little symbols came from and what they're actually called. items.title: English has an opposites problem
items.description: Let's explore contronyms. And 🌏 get an exclusive NordVPN deal + 4 months extra here → https://nordvpn.com/robwordsvpn It’s risk-free with Nord’s 30-day money-back guarantee! ✌️ "Fast", "clip", "sanction", "leave"... can have two opposing meanings. How does that happen? In this video, let's explore the self-contradictory words known as “contronyms”. The Vikings, the Romans and the Normans all play their parts, so let's get to the tales behind the antithesis. Also, YouTuber Evan Edinger joins us to look at some transatlantic linguistic clashes: words like "quite" that mean one thing in British English and something else very different in American English. items.title: Almost no names are 'English'
items.description: Did you know there are only a handful of truly English names? In this video, let's explore where our names really come from: from the Anglo-Saxon 'Edward' and 'Alfred' to Norman 'William' and 'Richard', and biblical names such as 'John', 'Mary' and 'Jacob'. Along the way we’ll uncover surprising connections between names across languages and centuries.
